cards.title: High-quality AI content workflow: negative keyword list, tone-of-voice doc, preliminary-question prompt
cards.summary: A repeatable AI-assisted writing workflow that keeps output on-brand and well-sourced instead of generic AI fluff.
cards.use_when: You need to produce blog or category copy for your store at volume without it reading like generic AI content.
steps: Build a negative keyword list: start from a general list of AI clichés ('in the ever-evolving world of', em dashes, 'delve'), and keep appending phrases the model produces that you dislike. Re-attach this list to every generation.

Build a tone-of-voice document: collect 1+ pieces of content you wrote yourself and liked (blog post, email, LinkedIn post — engagement doesn't matter, only that it sounds like you). Paste them into a tone-of-voice GPT, read the resulting document, and correct anything you disagree with before saving it as a Google Doc.
Use the copywriting prompt with the keyword/question inserted in brackets, and attach both the negative keyword list and the tone-of-voice doc.
Instruct the prompt to ask you preliminary questions before writing. Answer them fully; the source explicitly states better input produces better output. Ask it to research and cite sources.
Have it produce an outline first, amend the outline, then request the full draft. Keep an FAQ section at the end.
Before publishing, read it yourself as the subject matter expert, replace fluffy phrasing, and add a first-hand experience or story into the relevant section.
caveats: Source's position: search engines penalize low-quality content, not AI content; do not blindly copy 100% AI sites that happen to rank.
For financial topics ('your money, your life' category), backlinking to high-quality sources is described as non-negotiable.
Never publish straight from the draft; editing and adding original experience is required.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Surviving AI search overviews: unique voice, sourced data, simple language, visuals
cards.summary: GEO principles for getting cited in AI overviews, GPT search and Perplexity, summarised from a Princeton GEO paper cited in the source.
cards.use_when: You are writing store content (category pages, buying guides, blog posts) that needs to be picked up by AI search results, not just classic SERPs.
steps: Write in a distinct voice rather than neutral corporate filler — the source frames uniqueness as a core GEO lever.
Answer the actual questions your audience asks; feed those questions straight from your keyword/question research into the brief.

Back statements with specific data instead of vague claims, and link to the original source of that data. The source's example: replace 'drinking 2L of water a day is healthy' with a specific, cited statistic.
Write at roughly an eighth-grade reading level; the source describes this as making content approachable, not dumbing it down. Cut fluff and get to the point immediately.
Always produce an initial draft, then polish by removing unnecessary words.
Add supporting visuals (e.g. diagrams, comparison charts) to make the point easier to grasp.
caveats: The ~40% average increase in AI-overview visibility comes from a Princeton GEO paper the source cites; treat it as a published-research figure, not a guarantee for your store.
No specific benchmarks for your niche were supplied.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Add supporting visuals to content with Napkin.ai and ship them as WebP
cards.summary: Turn a text section into a simple explanatory visual and upload it in an optimised image format.
cards.use_when: A product or blog section is hard to grasp from text alone and would benefit from a diagram before you publish the page.
steps: Take the passage you want to visualise and paste it into Napkin.ai (new napkin), select all of the text so the tool knows what to reference.
Generate the visualisation and review the suggested formats (the source got a pros-and-cons comparison for equity home loans). Adjust styling if needed.
Download the result as PNG, then convert it to WebP before uploading. The source identifies PNGs as a common cause of heavy pages.
Place the visual under the relevant section of the article.
Add an FAQ block at the end, which the source has the prompt append automatically.
caveats: Tool UI and free-tier limits change — verify the current Napkin.ai interface and free plan before relying on it.
The source notes you can also generate images via the cluster tool's Stability AI integration with a chosen style preset.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Two types of links every content page needs: external citation + internal money page
cards.summary: Content that ranks and converts must cite external sources for its claims and internally link to the commercial page it supports.
cards.use_when: You're publishing a blog or guide for your store and want it to drive traffic to category or service pages.
steps: Identify every factual claim in the draft and link out to the original source of that data. The source treats this as mandatory for financial topics and best practice generally.
Identify the commercial pages on your site the article should support (e.g. a service page or product page for the topic) and add contextual internal links to them from the relevant sections.
If you're operating a service site that offers the thing the article is about, link the article to that offer page so the article acts as a supporting asset.
If you have a genuine personal story on the topic, insert it into the article — the source calls this an extra tick in the ranking box.
When generating at scale, set citations to inline links rather than footnotes and review the tool's internal links before exporting.
caveats: The source frames internal linking with a metaphor (a blog post without internal links is a room without doors), not a numeric rule.
Optional publishing tools may only natively connect to WordPress and Webflow — verify the current integrations.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Pillar-and-satellite content plan for an ecommerce or service store
cards.summary: Structure a topic cluster around one main page plus supporting articles that all link back to it.
cards.use_when: You're planning the content calendar or site architecture for a store and want topical authority around a core product or destination.
steps: Pick the pillar page — a main commercial page (services page, category page, destination page). The source's example is a travel agency's 'traveling to Tulum, how to get there and services' page.
Brainstorm the smaller questions buyers ask about that topic; these become the supporting articles.
Ensure every supporting article links back to the pillar page, and the pillar links out to relevant support articles.
Plan these pages into your sitemap/wireframe before building, using a spreadsheet to track page, keyword, and status.
Accept that any number of pages is fine as long as each answers a distinct search intent — the source states you can't really have too many pages if each answers intent.
For an ecommerce store the same structure applies: main pages, subpages, and sub-subpages, each mapped to a buyer question.
caveats: The source acknowledges an argument that large page counts waste crawl resources, but reports it has worked well across niches in their experience — plan accordingly rather than copying blindly.
Cited as source opinion from practitioner experience, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Scale content production with a cluster tool (Machined AI workflow)
cards.summary: Use a clustering tool to generate a batch of interrelated posts in your tone of voice, then edit them rather than publishing raw output.
cards.use_when: You need many supporting articles produced quickly for a category, destination or service cluster.
steps: Sign in and connect your own OpenAI API key if you have one (create it in the OpenAI playground dashboard under API keys, save the secret key immediately since you can't see it again, and make sure your account has credits).
Open 'clusters' → 'create content' and set the topic (e.g. a subtopic like home equity loans), audience (the more defined the better), language, region, and engine version.
Start with a limited cluster size (the source uses 10) and let it research search intent and suggest keywords and titles with estimated search volume.
Review the suggested titles and remove ones that don't fit the deliverable — e.g. skip a 'home loan calculator' post if the tool won't build the calculator for you.
Assign a content type per post (informational, ultimate guide, list, roundup, comparison) and vary them.
Use the custom brief field for any first-hand knowledge or specific points you want covered.
Set the author/tone of voice — you can either pick a preset or build a custom one by pasting your own writing sample for analysis.
Set the research section: include domains you want cited, add competitors to exclude, optionally point it at a specific site to crawl, and choose inline links over footnotes.

Choose the model. The source tested both a stronger and a lighter model and reports that as long as you fill in all the prior information, both produce good content; the stronger model costs roughly $0.50 per blog post in their experience and the lighter one is faster.
Edit the generated posts directly in the platform, review the inline source links and any internal links between cluster posts, then copy, export or publish as a draft to your CMS.
caveats: API costs and model names change — verify current pricing and model availability before promising output.
Native CMS publishing was only available for WordPress and Webflow at recording time; otherwise copy-paste.
The source explicitly frames this as producing ten editable drafts in the time one post used to take, not as replacement writing: 'I don't want you just to generate regurgitated AI fluff.'
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Don't buy 'our content ranks number one' promises — learn the fundamentals instead
cards.summary: Tool choice matters less than understanding what makes content good; distrust tools advertising guaranteed rankings.
cards.use_when: You're evaluating an AI content tool or agency for your store's content production.
steps: Judge the tool against the fundamentals you already know: does it let you define audience, tone of voice, sources, internal links, and custom briefs?
If you prefer a different AI content tool, the source says use it — the workflow transfers.
Ignore absolute ranking promises. The source states plainly that a tool claiming 'our content will rank you number one' is wrong.
Budget editing time regardless of tool. The generation is the speed gain; due diligence and added value are still your job.
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion, not a measured claim.
Adjacent claim from the source: some 100% AI-generated sites rank well, but they recommend not trying to copy them because it likely won't work for you.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Local SEO fundamentals: Google Business Profile, citations, locality on site
cards.summary: Three non-negotiable pillars that drive local visibility for a store with a physical presence or service area.
cards.use_when: You run a local store or service-area business and need a prioritised local SEO plan.
steps: Google Business Profile: claim and verify (requires a legitimate physical office), then fill in primary and secondary categories, description, opening date, phone, service areas, and business attributes.
Local citations: get listed in relevant directories as local backlinks, keeping NAP (name, address, phone) identical across all of them.
Website locality: add the location keyword to every service page, title tag and heading.
Keep the services and locations you claim identical between your website and your Google Business Profile.
caveats: The source says claiming a profile is getting harder due to scam attempts; a legitimate business is fine.
They note local SEO contains much more than these three items, but present these as the actionable core.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Optimise the Google Business Profile: categories, images to 100, weekly posts, reviews
cards.summary: Operate the GBP like an active social account, with category accuracy, image volume, posts and easy review capture.
cards.use_when: You've claimed your store's GBP and want it to actually drive calls, direction requests and site visits.
steps: Find primary and secondary categories using a category-finder GPT trained on Google's official category CSV. Add as many relevant categories as Google allows; verification may be pending. Categories differ by country.

Edit the description (must fit under 750 characters), opening date, phone, chat option, and service area. Add suburb-level service areas, not just the main city — and be careful to pick the correct suburb in the correct country.
Add attributes from both the business and the crowd (e.g. woman-owned, LGBTQ+ friendly) where accurate.

Upload a logo and cover photo, then upload fresh images regularly with the goal of 100 images. The source cites a BrightLocal study showing strong correlation between 100+ image profiles and website visits, direction requests and calls, with the effect rising sharply past 100.

Post at least once a week. Rewrite a blog post into a GBP update with a prompt specifying your tone of voice and under 1,450 characters (to leave leeway under the 1,500 limit), attach an image, and set the CTA button to 'learn more' linking to the blog post to drive site traffic. Also use offer and event post types for sales or events.

Add services under the services section, including services that don't exist as a GBP category (the source's examples: therapeutic gardening, NDIS support coordination) — and make sure the services listed on GBP also appear on the website.
Add a direct booking link (form, call, or Calendar link) if you offer one.
Get customers or a friend to ask your most frequently asked questions in the Q&A section so you can answer them — you asking them yourself is pointless.

Request reviews using the review link and its QR code. Print the QR code on pamphlets and cards. The source's strongest finding: asking for reviews in person after service beats every automated text-message approach they've tried.
Respond to both negative and positive reviews.
caveats: The 100-image figure comes from a BrightLocal study cited by the source; treat it as a heuristic. The source sets the goal at 100 images.
Descriptions over ~750 characters won't fit.
The source notes Google Business Profile is one of the few assets that keeps generating leads even if your website goes down.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Running a local citation campaign with NAP consistency
cards.summary: Find, submit and track local directory listings so the same name, address and phone appear everywhere.
cards.use_when: You're building local trust for a new store or a store that has changed name, address or phone number.
steps: Use a local-listings GPT that takes your business URL (or business description) and returns relevant free directories — first niche/industry-specific ones, then broader general ones (the source's examples for Australia: True Local, Hotfrog, Start Local, Aussie Web).
Put the results in a Google Sheet with columns for directory name, URL, and a status dropdown marked 'done' as you complete each, so you don't resubmit.
On each directory, find 'add your business' (main menu or footer), enter your details, and keep the name, address and phone number byte-identical across all listings.
Do this quarterly-to-annually rather than monthly — the source says once every six months to a year is probably enough — and keep them updated.

If you don't want to do it manually or you run many locations, a citation-building service can do it; the source says check the service supports your target country first, and notes costs around $3.20 per site via BrightLocal at the time of the recording.
Agencies commonly resell this with a markup (the source mentions adding roughly 50% or $10 per site).
caveats: Pricing and directory availability change — verify current rates and coverage.
If a citation service doesn't cover your country, the source suggests a freelancer is acceptable for this task since it is not complicated.
The source calls this the only service of its kind they'd personally trust, which is a presenter preference, not a measured comparison.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Localise on-site content: put the location into titles, H1s and metadata
cards.summary: A .com.au domain alone isn't granular enough — every service page and heading should name the city.
cards.use_when: You're optimising service or category pages for a specific city or region.
steps: Take each service page and add the local keyword to the service name: 'therapeutic gardening' becomes 'therapeutic gardening in Melbourne' (the source's example).
Apply the same change to the title tag — target roughly 45–61 characters — and to the H1/headings, which in the example only said 'therapeutic gardening'.

Run a website-localisation GPT/analyzer over the site: confirm the services and the target locations, then get a page-by-page review of where local keywords are missing from the homepage, H-tags and titles.
Fix the flagged gaps, then cross-check that the services and locations you claim on the site match your Google Business Profile.
Note the source's caution about ambiguous place names: verify the suburb AND country (Vermont exists in both the USA and Victoria, Australia).
caveats: The source says not to trust the analyzer blindly, but it gives a good starting point.
Brand tone statements like 'empowering your dog to success' are called out as not being location-definitive and therefore insufficient on their own.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx

cards.title: Technical SEO scope plus speed checks with two tools
cards.summary: What falls under technical SEO, and how to measure page speed without a biased result.
cards.use_when: You're auditing your store's site and need to decide what to check first and what to escalate to a developer.
steps: Define scope: the source considers theme changes and anything requiring code to be the web developer's responsibility, not the SEO's.
Test loading speed with two tools to get an unbiased read — the source recommends GTmetrix and Google PageSpeed Insights (both free tiers are enough for a few sites).

Read GTmetrix's grade. Below a B means there's a problem to sort out. The source describes their test page loading at 1.9 seconds as good, and anything slower than 3 seconds as costing conversions — 'leaving money on the table'.
Note that your own site feels fast because browsers cache files locally; first-time visitors have to fetch images and CSS from the host, so judge by the tools, not your own experience.
Use GTmetrix's report to identify heavy assets — the source's example was a video that could be compressed without losing much quality.
Use PageSpeed Insights for the mobile vs desktop split, and optimise mobile first since Google sets a mobile-first standard.
Benchmark against competitors: the source's framing is that competing in a very competitive niche with a technically weak site is like entering Formula 1 in a Prius.
caveats: The 3-second and B-grade thresholds are the source's heuristics, not measured conversion benchmarks.
GTmetrix server location can only be changed on the paid version; the source says it doesn't matter much for an unbiased read.
Mobile generally dominates traffic except for genuinely B2B businesses — the source says to optimise mobile first.
cards.source_name: Complete SEO Course (3 Hours)_ Rank #1 AI Search _ Prompts Included.docx
